doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

title: Blindfold test: Eddie Harris and Freedom Jazz Dance
summary: Billy Higgins's drumming on the original and Harris as an unsung genius and electronics pioneer.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well let me see if I can negotiate this.
Now this tune is all one change? Is that the idea?
Um hum. Yeah I could talk about this one all day long. Yeah. Eddie Harris.

Yeah. The original “Freedom Jazz Dance.” Boy there’s so many things we could talk about. What I usually point out to people, and particularly my students when I usually bring a recording of this in, because most young students when they learn “Freedom Jazz Dance” they learn Miles’ version of it. And they’ve never heard this version, the original, and what it’s really about. The real catalyst on this recording is Billy Higgins. Because you hear the whole tradition of black music in his playing on this, from New Orleans forward. You hear that second line, you hear Congo Square, you hear swing, you hear funk. It’s dancing. It’s all about dance. And he really — I remember listening to this record once about fifteen years ago and I used to listen to it over and over and over and over. And just to listen to Billy Higgins’ snare drum on this record, just his snare. It’s like a symphony. Because it keeps developing, it keeps going, it keeps opening up. And it is what is propelling Eddie and everybody else to play what they play. And most bass players don’t know the original bass line that Ron is playing, just that one simple figure but it’s what makes it. And Eddie, to me who is the unsung genius of saxophone and one of the unsung geniuses of this music, and he’s probably been one of the biggest influences on me, one of the first people, well probably the first guy that I idolized so to speak, even before I could even pick up a saxophone, I used to love his records. I love him still but he covered the whole history of music. When you listen to all those different records he did in the sixties, where he’s doing “Breakfast at Tiffany’s” or “Exodus,” and then “Freedom Jazz Dance,” and then with his work with the electronics, which we talk about electronics and man this guy was ahead of everybody when it came to electronics, you know all the things he did: reed trumpet, saxophone mouthpiece on the trumpet, and that recording of “Oleo” where he’s playing the tenor saxophone with a trombone mouthpiece.
That one I’m not aware of. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
